chapter_theme: The Buddha himself sets out the aggregates (feeling, cognition, activity, their momentary arising, the soul as a name for them, and his four truths), and Neelakesi vows to destroy his view and answers that inseparable parts need a bearer, that a thing is known only through its qualities, that the eight constituents of matter put water in fire, and that his accounts of cognition and will contradict themselves or regress into the void.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in this sarukkam

488.reading: The Buddha tells Neelakesi that the feelings are three: pleasure, the pain that brings distress, and a middle feeling that comes from what is neither good nor evil deed.
488.nuance: This opens the Buddha's own account of the aggregates in the sarukkam, with feeling (வேதனை) first; the neutral feeling is tied here to deed that is neither good nor evil (line 3), a causal link the verse states in passing. Neelakesi answers the separateness of feeling in 505.

claims.claim: feeling is of three kinds: pleasant, painful and neither
the neutral feeling arises from deed that is neither good nor evil

489.reading: The Buddha says that cognitions arise when the five senses and the mind meet their objects, and that perceptions are what is named in these six; this, he says, is his way.
489.nuance: Cognition (அறிவு) and perception (குறி) are both defined by the six doors, with no knower behind them; 507 to 509 attack exactly this, asking how six cognitions can be counted if only one occurs at a time.

claims.claim: cognition is sixfold, arising when the five senses and the mind meet their objects, with no knower besides

490.reading: The Buddha says that the activities called wholesome and unwholesome are divided into many kinds by the fruit of deeds and are done by mind, speech and body, and asks who among the deluded could know them.
490.nuance: குயலா குயலம் is the Pali-Sanskrit pair kusala and akusala, and வசி and காயம் are speech and body; the verse names the formations by the three doors of action. Lines 3 and 4 (மயலா மனமே, மயலா ரிதாவை) are hard to divide, so the closing question is a reading.

claims.claim: deeds are wholesome or unwholesome and are done by mind, speech and body

491.reading: The Buddha says the five aggregates arise together and perish within a single moment, as the tip of a flame on a lamp does.
491.nuance: The flame tip (சுடர் நுதி) is the image Kundalakesi used for the same doctrine in 177 (எரிநுதி). The claim that all five arise at once is what 506 turns against him, by giving the aggregates a causal order.

claims.claim: the five aggregates arise together and perish within one moment

492.reading: The Buddha says that as five fingers placed together are called a hand, so the five aggregates together are what is called a living soul.
492.nuance: The soul becomes a collective name, not a thing; 495 takes the same fingers (there a fist, முட்டி) and argues that what holds them together must be a bearer of qualities.

claims.claim: a soul is only the name for the five aggregates taken together, as 'hand' is for five fingers

493.reading: The Buddha ends his account: the aggregates are impermanent, painful and impure, and no soul is to be established in them; these four are his truth, and those who know them so reach release whatever they do.
493.nuance: The four named here are impermanence, suffering, impurity (அசுவம், asubha) and no soul, which is a Jain poet's version of the Buddha's 'four truths'; the Buddhist Manimekalai (30) gives the four truths as suffering, its cause, release and its cause. எவையே செய்தும் ('whatever they do') may be the poet's barb that knowledge alone, not conduct, is said to free, the point the monk made in 259. Line 2 (நாட்டிலங்காட்டமிலை) is hard to divide.
493.event: The Buddha finishes setting out his doctrine of the aggregates to Neelakesi.

claims.claim: the aggregates are impermanent, painful and impure, and there is no soul
those who understand these four truths reach release whatever they do

494.reading: Having heard of the many-natured five aggregates and of the false soul that is a mere name for their loose unity, the lily-garlanded Neelakesi says she will destroy his view, like those who burn down a hut.
494.nuance: பொய்யுயிர் ('false soul') is the narrator's summary of the Buddha's position, and காட்சி ('view', line 4) is the word Jains use for right or wrong faith, so destroying his காட்சி is a matter of doctrine, not only of debate. The simile வேட்டக் குரம்பை சுடுபவர் is unclear: the hut of hunters, or a hut one has cherished.
494.event: Neelakesi hears the Buddha out and vows to destroy his view.

495.reading: Neelakesi argues that since he calls the aggregate inseparable, there must be one bearer whose qualities they are; otherwise, split apart, each must be a separate thing, as the five fingers in the fist he cited are.
495.nuance: The Buddha's example cuts both ways: either the aggregates are one thing's qualities (குணம் of a குணி, the Jain soul) or they are five things and no 'person' at all. The Buddha said 'hand' in 492 and Neelakesi says 'fist', so the example may have stood in a lost or differently worded verse.

claims.claim: the aggregates form one inseparable whole
parts that are inseparable must be the qualities of one bearer, and that bearer is the soul

496.reading: Neelakesi argues that things have both their nature and their action, joined yet distinct, and asks what fault there is in establishing the soul from its nature.
496.nuance: Line 1 is corrupt and the argument is read from lines 2 to 4; தன்மை and கருமம் (nature and function) return in 501.

claims.claim: a thing has both a nature and an action, so the soul can be established from its nature

497.reading: Neelakesi says that as he gives hardness and support as the marks of earth, she gives knowing and seeing as the marks of the soul; if earth is established, so is the soul, man of great wisdom.
497.nuance: உணர்வு and காட்சி are the Jain pair of knowledge and perception that define the soul; the argument is one of parity, using the Buddhist's own way of defining an element by its marks. பெரிய பிரச்சையினாய் (great prajna) is ironic.

claims.claim: earth is known by its marks of hardness and support
if earth is established by its marks, the soul is established by its marks of knowing and seeing

498.reading: Neelakesi says he holds there is no earth apart from hardness and no soul apart from cognition, yet says that earth persists and bears things; she calls him the compassionate one who toiled for others through every aeon.
498.nuance: The address in line 4 repeats the praise Kundalakesi gave her teacher in 176 (அயலார்க்கே துன்புற்றான்), now spoken to the Buddha himself in a verse that charges him with contradiction.

claims.claim: there is no earth apart from hardness and no soul apart from cognition

499.reading: Neelakesi argues that if earth is nothing but hardness he cannot make great earth known, and yet he demands to be shown the soul; has any thing ever been made clear except through its qualities?

claims.claim: nothing is ever made known except through its qualities, so the soul need not be shown apart from them

500.reading: Neelakesi says that he claims to accept no contradiction, yet has not given up the eight he took as real, which puts water in fire unchanged, a contradiction plain to sight; is this, Buddha, the wisdom that says only incoherent things?
500.nuance: அட்டகம் ('the eight') is read as the eight constituents that the Buddhist account holds are always found together in matter, so that water is present even in fire; the verse names the eight only by number. திட்ட விரோதம் is the logician's term for a claim contradicted by what is seen.

claims.claim: the eight constituents of matter are always found together
a doctrine that puts water within fire is contradicted by what is seen

501.reading: Neelakesi argues that if nature and function belong to the elements, then since the four elements are opposites present within one another, each would destroy the other's nature and use.
501.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure (தானென்னைவே றின்மை), so the step from the first half to the conclusion is a reading.

claims.claim: if the four opposed elements are present in each other, each loses its nature and its use

502.reading: Neelakesi asks why one says 'this is a town, this a forest', and how, if all are present together, one could say 'this is water, this is fire'; if the eight are everywhere, even giving a name goes wrong.
502.nuance: The town and forest are the ordinary case of naming by what is there; the octad, she argues, leaves no ground for naming one element rather than another.

claims.claim: if all eight constituents are present everywhere, nothing can be named as one element rather than another

503.reading: Neelakesi takes up his answer that though the constituents stand together he names a thing by the one that predominates, and dismisses the reasonings he offers; with this she ends a stretch of her reply.
503.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (புக்கனதாம் பொறியானின்புலமன்றிப் பொய்யெனத்தா னக்கனர் சாக) are obscure; they seem to say that what enters through the senses is called false, and that others laugh at such methods, but the sense cannot be fixed. என்றாள் closes a speech, though 504 continues in her voice.

claims.claim: a compound is named after the constituent that predominates in it

504.reading: Neelakesi says that apart from the eight with form, it is impossible for all that falls within the five aggregates to join, touch and produce one another; deluding the attached with illusions, she says, he drives his chariot through empty space.
504.nuance: அவகாயத்துத் தேரை ('a chariot in empty space') is read as an image of an argument that moves without ground; the verse is hard and the reading is offered tentatively.

claims.claim: the formless aggregates cannot combine by contact as material things do

505.reading: Neelakesi argues that the three feelings remain in him too, and that if the many activities he named before are examined, feeling is only their outgrowth and nothing apart from them.
505.nuance: She makes the move she made against Kundalakesi in 194, folding feeling into activity, and so denies feeling the standing of a separate aggregate. Line 2 (கரிவே தனையவர் காமுறு காமம்) is obscure.

claims.claim: feeling is not a separate aggregate but an outgrowth of activity

506.reading: Neelakesi argues that activity is made by cognition and feeling by activity, and that cognition bears a trace of its object; so the aggregates stand in an order of cause and effect, and things that lose their connection become other and other and cannot be had.
506.nuance: Read against 491, the causal order cognition, activity, feeling tells against the claim that all five arise in one moment. Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe.

claims.claim: cognition produces activity and activity produces feeling, so the aggregates are cause and effect, not simultaneous

507.reading: Neelakesi asks how, when only one of the six cognitions occurs at a time, he knows that the other five exist; and if he says they exist though sunk from view, what fault is there in affirming the soul by the same method?

claims.claim: only one of the six cognitions occurs at a time
if cognitions can exist without appearing, the soul can be affirmed by the same reasoning

508.reading: Neelakesi says that he holds that when one cognition is present the departed ones cannot be perceived even by name, that no two cognitions exist at once, and also that the six exist together; his words, she says, destroy one another.
508.nuance: ஓருணர்வே உடையீர் ('you who have only one cognition') turns his doctrine into an insult: a mind that holds one thing at a time cannot see its own contradiction.

claims.claim: there are never two cognitions at once
the six cognitions exist together

509.reading: Neelakesi takes up the answer that cognition occurs as one because the knower stands alone in it, and argues that if the six are distinct by their own existence, going out to their objects and meeting them would suit a knower.
509.nuance: The verse names a knower (அறிவான், line 2), which is what the Jain wants the Buddhist to concede; the construal of lines 3 and 4 is uncertain.

claims.claim: cognitions that occur one at a time point to a single knower

510.reading: Neelakesi argues that if he says all things are not known at once for lack of will, then a separate will for each would bring them all together, and one will for all makes will the bearer of qualities; he is, she says, like the carpenter who in fear cries 'thief'.
510.nuance: A single will that governs every cognition is a soul under another name, which is why the carpenter of the proverb, who cries out and so gives himself away, fits; the proverb itself (தச்சனஞ் சிச்சா ரகழ்கள்வன்) is obscure.

claims.claim: cognitions do not all arise at once because will is lacking
a single will governing all cognitions would be a bearer of qualities, a soul under another name

511.reading: Neelakesi argues that if his will perishes at every arising, knowledge cannot grow from excellence to excellence; if each pot just milked is tasted, how could the vessels be full of milk, curd and buttermilk?
511.nuance: Milk, curd and buttermilk are one substance through its changes; the image asks for something that lasts through change, which momentary perishing denies. The phrasing of lines 3 and 4 is hard and the image's exact point is a reading.

claims.claim: if every moment perishes wholly, knowledge cannot grow by accumulation

512.reading: Neelakesi argues that if every cognition arises by way of will, and his will has no will before it, positing one for it too makes a regress without end; so there is no escaping it: his expansion ends in the void.
512.nuance: The void (சூனியம்) here is the end of a failed argument, not a goal; it echoes Neelakesi's charge in 263 that the Buddha taught a void release.

claims.claim: all cognitions arise by way of will
if every will needs a prior will, there is an infinite regress

links.note: 491 says the five aggregates arise together in one moment; 506 gives them an order in which cognition makes activity and activity makes feeling.
links.teaches: Neelakesi uses the Buddhist's own causal chain against his doctrine of simultaneity: if one aggregate produces another, they cannot all be born and die in the same instant.

links.note: The Buddha calls the five aggregates a soul only as five fingers are called a hand; Neelakesi says the fingers' unity needs a bearer, or else they are five things.
links.teaches: The Buddha's chosen example becomes the Jain's evidence: an analogy for a mere name is turned into a case of qualities that need one substance.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the collective name (body, water, country) as a Buddhist mode of speech; the Neelakesi's Buddha calls the soul such a name, like 'hand' for five fingers.
links.teaches: The Jain poet gives his Buddha a doctrine the Buddhist epic itself states, so here the polemic reports Buddhist teaching recognisably before answering it.

links.note: The Neelakesi's Buddha calls impermanence, suffering, impurity and no-soul his four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives the four truths as suffering, its cause, release and release's cause.
links.teaches: Holding the two lists together shows the Jain epic replacing the Buddhist's path of cause and cure with four bare marks of things, so that release seems to follow from seeing alone; this depends on reading நான்மை in 493 as the four truths.

links.note: The Buddha says those who know the four truths reach release whatever they do; the monk in 259 says only the mind counts and evil conduct is not evil karma.
links.teaches: The monk's excuse in the earlier debate is given a source in the Buddha's own words here, so the poet makes the founder answerable for the disciple's conduct; this rests on reading எவையே செய்தும் as 'whatever they do'.

links.note: Kundalakesi praised her teacher as one who suffered only for others; Neelakesi addresses the Buddha as the compassionate one who toiled for others through every aeon, in a verse that charges him with contradiction.
links.teaches: The Buddhist's chief title of praise returns in the Jain's mouth as an ironic address, so the founder's compassion is set beside the incoherence of his doctrine.

links.note: Against Kundalakesi, Neelakesi folded feeling, perception and volition into knowing; against the Buddha she folds feeling into activity.
links.teaches: The Jain reply to the five aggregates is the same in both debates: reduce them until only knowing and form remain, which is the Jain pair of soul and non-soul.

links.note: The Buddha counts six cognitions at the six doors; Neelakesi asks how the five not occurring can be known to exist, and says their hidden existence licenses a soul.
links.teaches: Counting six kinds of cognition already assumes something that holds the unused ones, so the Buddhist's own enumeration is made to imply the abiding knower he denies.

links.note: Against Kundalakesi, Neelakesi said that if nothing of one moment is in the next, knowing and speaking are impossible; against the Buddha she says that if will perishes at each arising, knowledge cannot grow.
links.teaches: The argument against momentariness moves from memory to learning: the first debate asked how anything is known, this one how anything is learned.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain says gram keeps its nature when cooked into a dish; the Neelakesi's Jain asks how milk, curd and buttermilk could fill the vessels if nothing lasts.
links.teaches: Both epics give the Jain the same proof from the kitchen, a substance that persists through its changes; the Buddhist epic reports it unanswered there, and the Jain epic aims it at the Buddha's momentariness.

links.note: In 263 Neelakesi grieves for the Buddha who taught a void release; in 512 she argues that his account of will ends in the void through infinite regress.
links.teaches: The void is charged twice, once as a goal no one could want and once as the end of a regress, so the Jain treats Buddhist emptiness as both a bad hope and a failed argument.

links.note: Neelakesi says the Buddha's reasoning collapses into the void; the Siddhar tells his listener that all arising deeds are seen to be void, appearing without appearing in pure space.
links.teaches: For the Jain debater reaching the void is a reductio, for the Siddhar it is the seeing that frees; the same word marks defeat in one tradition and insight in the other.

gains.a: the Jain charge gains a witness that some Tamil teachers embraced the void as a goal, so the charge is aimed at a live position, not a straw one
gains.b: the Siddhar's void gains the objection it must meet, that a void reached by regress leaves nothing to know or hold

links.note: The Kural says understanding is seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever nature; Neelakesi says no thing has ever been made clear except through its qualities.
links.teaches: The Jain makes the couplet's 'whatever its nature' into a method: the true thing is reached through its qualities, not by stripping them away, which is why she can claim the soul is known by knowing and seeing.

gains.a: the debater's rule about qualities gains the Kural's claim that seeing the real thing is what understanding is for
gains.b: the couplet gains an answer to how the true thing is to be seen, which it leaves open

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: கந்தம் (491, 492), ஐங்கந்தம் (494)

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: a quality borne by a substance (குணி, its bearer); in the Jain argument a thing, the soul included, is known only through its qualities
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: குணம் (495), குணமுகத்தால் (499), குணி (495), குணிப்பொருள் (510)

source_issues: Verse 490, lines 3-4: மயலா மனமே வசிகா யத்தினா / மயலா ரிதாவை are hard to divide; குயலா குயலம் (line 1) stands for குசலம் அகுசலம்.
Verse 493, line 2: நாட்டிலங்காட்டமிலை is hard to divide.
Verse 496, line 1: பூதன்கும் புகுந்தே தெருல்லலுற் றயவற்றுக் is corrupt and cannot be construed; line 4 சாத மாமுயிர் may lack a syllable.
Verse 502, line 4: சொ;லுத has a stray semicolon for சொல்லுத.
Verse 503, lines 3-4 and verse 509, lines 3-4 are obscure in word division.
Verse 510, line 4: the proverb தச்சனஞ் சிச்சா ரகழ்கள்வன் is hard to divide (தச்சன் அஞ்சி?).
Verse 495 cites the Buddha's example as a fist (முட்டி), but 492 speaks of a hand (கை); the example may have stood in a verse now lost or differently worded.
